L9@P0: SUMMARY: This final rule upgrades NHTSA’s head restraint standard in order to
L10@P0: reduce whiplash injuries in rear collisions. For front seats, the rule establishes a higher
L11@P0: minimum height requirement, a requirement limiting the distance between the back of an
L12@P0: occupant’s head and the occupant’s head restraint, as well as a limit on the size of gaps
L13@P0: and openings within head restraints. The rule also establishes new strength and dynamic
L14@P0: compliance requirements, and amends most existing test procedures. In addition, the rule
L15@P0: establishes requirements for head restraints voluntarily installed in rear outboard
L16@P0: designated seating positions. The upgraded standard becomes mandatory for all vehicles
L17@P0: manufactured on or after September 1, 2008. Until that time, the manufacturers may
L18@P0: comply with the existing NHTSA standard, the upgraded NHTSA standard or the current
L19@P0: European regulations.

L79@P2: I. Executive Summary
L80@P2: This final rule upgrades Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 202, Head
L81@P2: Restraints (FMVSS No. 202). The standard, which seeks to reduce whiplash injuries in
L82@P2: rear collisions, currently requires head restraints for front outboard designated seating
L83@P2: positions in passenger cars and in light multipurpose passenger vehicles, trucks and
L84@P2: buses.
L85@P2-3: To provide better whiplash protection for a wider range of occupants, this rule 4
L86@P3: requires that front outboard head restraints meet more stringent height requirements.
L87@P3: Fixed front head restraints must be not less than 800 mm. In their lowest adjustment
L88@P3: position, adjustable head restraints must not be lower than 750 mm, and in their highest
L89@P3: position, they must be at least 800 mm. To reduce the distance that a vehicle occupant’s
L90@P3: head can be whipped backward in a rear end crash, this rule establishes new requirements
L91@P3: limiting backset in front seats, i.e., the distance between the back of a person’s head and
L92@P3: his or her head restraint, and limiting the size of gaps and openings in the restraints. The
L93@P3: rule also establishes new strength and position retention requirements. Finally, it
L94@P3: significantly amends the dynamic compliance test option currently in the standard to
L95@P3: encourage continued development and use of “active” head restraint systems because the
L96@P3: test is designed to allow a manufacturer the flexibility necessary to offer innovative
L97@P3: active head restraint designs while still ensuring a minimal level of head restraint
L98@P3: performance.
L99@P3: After a careful consideration of the public comments and further analysis of our
L100@P3: proposal to require head restraints in each rear outboard designated seating position, we
L101@P3: have decided not to adopt that proposal. In the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
L102@P3: (NPRM),1
L103@P3:  we expressed concern that the proposal had a high cost per equivalent life
L104@P3: saved. We have now made a more refined estimate of costs and benefits and found that
L105@P3: the cost per equivalent life saved for such a requirement is even greater than originally
L106@P3: thought. In response to the NPRM, several manufacturers raised visibility concerns
L107@P3: associated with mandatory rear head restraints in all vehicles. While not a universal
L108@P3: problem, we believe reduced visibility is a legitimate problem in some vehicles. Finally,
L109@P3: in commenting on the NPRM, vehicle manufacturers expressed concern that adoption of
L110@P3: 
L111@P3-4: 1 See 66 F.R. 968 (January 4, 2001). 5
L112@P4: the requirement would reduce vehicle utility by interfering with or even reducing the
L113@P4: ability to provide the sort of folding seats currently available in “multi-configuration”
L114@P4: vehicles such as vans and multipurpose vehicles. We believe that those concerns may
L115@P4: have some merit.
L116@P4: However, in order to ensure that head restraints voluntarily installed in rear
L117@P4: outboard seating positions do not pose a risk of exacerbating whiplash injuries, this final
L118@P4: rule requires that those head restraints meet certain height, strength, position retention,
L119@P4: and energy absorption requirements. NHTSA notes that the head restraint regulation of
L120@P4: the United Nations/Economic Commission for Europe (UN/ECE) similarly does not
L121@P4: mandate rear seat head restraints, but does regulates the performance of voluntarily
L122@P4: installed ones. The ECE regulation is discussed at greater length several paragraphs
L123@P4: below and in Appendix A.
L124@P4: In the future stages of our efforts to improve occupant protection in rear impacts,2
L125@P4: NHTSA intends to evaluate the performance of head restraints and seat backs as a single
L126@P4: system to protect occupants, just as they work in the real world, instead of evaluating
L127@P4: their performance separately as individual components. Accordingly, in making our
L128@P4: decisions about the upgraded requirements for head restraints in this final rule, we
L129@P4: sought, e.g., through upgrading our dynamic test procedure option, to make those
L130@P4: requirements consistent with the ultimate goal of adopting a method of comprehensively
L131@P4: evaluating the seating system.
L132@P4: This final rule harmonizes the FMVSS requirements for head restraints with the
L133@P4: head restraint regulation of the UN/ECE, except to the extent needed to provide increased
L134@P4: 
L135@P4: 2
L136@P4:  As part of this effort, NHTSA issued a final rule upgrading the performance of vehicle fuel systems in
L137@P4-5: rear impacts. (68 FR 67068, December 1, 2003). 6
L138@P5: safety for vehicle occupants or to facilitate enforcement.3 In some instances, a desire to
L139@P5: achieve increased safety in a cost effective manner made it necessary for us to go beyond
L140@P5: or take an approach different from that in the ECE regulation.
L141@P5: While some of the requirements of this final rule are more stringent than those of
L142@P5: the ECE regulation, the latter is functionally equivalent to the current FMVSS No. 202.4
L143@P5: For this reason, in the interim before the mandatory compliance date of this rule
L144@P5: (September 1, 2008), the agency is giving manufacturers the option of complying with
L145@P5: any of three alternatives: the existing FMVSS No. 202, the ECE 17, or the new, upgraded
L146@P5: FMVSS No. 202, designated as FMVSS No. 202a.5
L147@P5: The agency estimates that approximately 272,464 whiplash injuries occur
L148@P5: annually. This final rule will result in approximately 16,831 fewer whiplash injuries,
L149@P5: 15,272 involving front seat occupants and 1,559 involving rear seat occupants. The
L150@P5: estimated average cost in 2002 dollars, per vehicle, of meeting this rule will be $4.51 for
L151@P5: front seats, and $1.13 for rear seats currently equipped with head restraints, for a
L152@P5: combined cost of $5.42.6 The cost per year is estimated to be $70.1 million for front head
L153@P5: restraints and $14.1 million for optional rear head restraints, for a combined annual cost
L154@P5: of $84.2 million. This final rule is economically significant because we estimate that the
L155@P5: final rule will result in economic benefits in excess of $100 million.
L156@P5: 
L157@P5: 3
L158@P5:  The regulation, adopted by the UN/ECE’s Working Party 29, World Forum for Harmonization of Vehicle
L159@P5: Regulations, is ECE 17, Uniform Provisions concerning the Approval of Vehicles with regard to the Seats,
L160@P5: their Anchorages, and any Head Restraints
L161@P5: (http://www.unece.org/trans/main/wp29/wp29regs/r017r4e.pdf). A comparison of this final rule with ECE
L162@P5: 17 is in Appendix A.
L163@P5: 4
L164@P5:  We determined that the current FMVSS No. 202 is functionally equivalent to the applicable ECE
L165@P5: regulation using the method described in Appendix B of 49 CFR Part 553.
L166@P5: 5
L167@P5:  Once the FMVSS No. 202a becomes fully effective on September 1, 2008, it will be re-designated as
L168@P5: FMVSS No. 202.

L172@P6: II. Background
L173@P6: Vehicle manufacturers currently use three types of head restraints to meet the
L174@P6: requirements of FMVSS No. 202. The first type is the “integral head restraint,” which is
L175@P6: non-adjustable and is built into the seat. It typically consists of a seat back that extends
L176@P6: high enough to meet the height requirement of the standard. The second type is the
L177@P6: “adjustable” head restraint, which consists of a separate cushion that is attached to the
L178@P6: seat back, typically by a two sliding metal shafts. Adjustable head restraints typically
L179@P6: adjust vertically to accommodate different occupant seating heights. Some also provide
L180@P6: adjustments to allow the head restraint to be moved closer to the occupant’s head. The
L181@P6: third type is the active head restraint system, which deploys in the event of a collision to
L182@P6: minimize the potential for whiplash. During the normal vehicle operation, the active
L183@P6: head restraint system is retracted.
L184@P6: a. The Safety Concern
L185@P6:  Whiplash injuries are a set of common symptoms that occur in motor vehicle
L186@P6: crashes and involve the soft tissues of the head, neck and spine. Symptoms of pain in the
L187@P6: head, neck, shoulders, and arms may be present along with damage to muscles, ligaments
L188@P6: and vertebrae, but in many cases lesions are not evident. The onset of symptoms may be
L189@P6: delayed and may only last a few hours; however, in some cases, effects of the injury may
L190@P6: last for years or even be permanent. The relatively short-term symptoms are associated
L191@P6: with muscle and ligament trauma, while the long-term ones are associated with nerve
L192@P6-7: damage. 8
L193@P7: Based on National Analysis Sampling System (NASS) data, we estimate that
L194@P7: between 1988 and 1996, 805,581 whiplash injuries7 occurred annually in crashes
L195@P7: involving passenger cars and LTVs (light trucks, multipurpose passenger vehicles, and
L196@P7: vans). Of these whiplash injuries, 272,464 occurred as a result of rear impacts. For rear
L197@P7: impact crashes, the average cost of whiplash injuries in 2002 dollars is $9,994 (which
L198@P7: includes $6,843 in economic costs and $3,151 in quality of life impacts, but not property
L199@P7: damage), resulting in a total annual cost of approximately $2.7 billion.
L200@P7: b. Understanding Whiplash
L201@P7: Although whiplash injuries can occur in any kind of crash, an occupant’s chances
L202@P7: of sustaining this type of injury are greatest in rear-end collisions. When a vehicle is
L203@P7: struck from behind, typically several things occur in quick succession to an occupant of
L204@P7: that vehicle. First, from the occupant's frame of reference, the back of the seat moves
L205@P7: forward into his or her torso, straightening the spine and forcing the head to rise
L206@P7: vertically. Second, as the seat pushes the occupant’s body forward, the unrestrained head
L207@P7: tends to lag behind. This causes the neck to change shape, first taking on an S-shape and
L208@P7: then bending backward. Third, the forces on the neck accelerate the head, which catches
L209@P7: up with--and, depending on the seat back stiffness and if the occupant is using a shoulder
L210@P7: belt, passes--the restrained torso. This motion of the head and neck, which is like the lash
L211@P7: of a whip, gives the resulting neck injuries their popular name.
L212@P7: Previous regulatory approach. As discussed in the NPRM preceding this final
L213@P7: rule, a historical examination of head restraint standards in this country indicates that the
L214@P7: focus has been the prevention of neck hyperextension (the rearward movement of the
L215@P7: head and neck over a large range of motion relative to the torso), as opposed to
L216@P7:

L220@P8: FMVSS No. 202 was General Services Administration (GSA) Standard 515/22, which
L221@P8: applied to vehicles purchased by the U.S. Government and went into effect on October 1,
L222@P8: 1967. GSA 515/22 required that the top of the head restraint achieve a height 700 mm
L223@P8: (27.5 inches (in)) above the H-point.8
L224@P8:  Also in 1967, research using staged 48 kilometer
L225@P8: per hour (kph) (30 mile per hour, mph) crashes concluded that a head restraint 711 mm
L226@P8: (28 in) above the H-point was adequate to prevent neck hyperextension of a 95th
L227@P8: percentile male. FVMSS No. 202, which became effective on January 1, 1969, required
L228@P8: that head restraints be at least 700 mm (27.5 in) above the seating reference point or limit
L229@P8: the relative angle between the head and the torso to 45 degrees or less during a dynamic
L230@P8: test.

L237@P8:  By contrast,
L238@P8: another study showed significant increase in injury and duration of symptoms when

L250@P9: In addition, the persistence of whiplash injuries in the current fleet of vehicles
L251@P9: indicates that the existing height requirement is not sufficient to prevent excessive
L252@P9: movement of the head and neck relative to the torso for some people. Specifically, the
L253@P9: head restraints do not effectively limit rearward movement of the head of a person at least
L254@P9: as tall as the average occupant. Research indicates that taller head restraints would better
L255@P9: prevent whiplash injuries because at heights of 750 to 800 mm, the head restraint can
L256@P9: more effectively limit the movement of the head and neck.
L257@P9: In a recent report from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS), Farmer,
L258@P9: Wells, and Lund examined automobile insurance claims to determine the rates of neck
L259@P9: injuries in rear end crashes for vehicles with the improved geometric fit of head restraints
L260@P9: (reduced backset and increased head restraint height).11 Their data indicate that these
L261@P9: improved head restraints are reducing the risk of whiplash injury. Specifically, there was
L262@P9: an 18 percent reduction in injury claims. Similarly, NHTSA computer generated models
L263@P9: have shown that the reduction of the backset and an increase in the height of the head
L264@P9: restraint reduces the level of neck loading and relative head-to-torso motion that may be
L265@P9: related to the incidence of whiplash injuries.12
L266@P9: With respect to impact speeds, research and injury rate data indicate that whiplash
L267@P9: may occur as a result of head and neck movements insufficient to cause hyperextension.

L274@P10: Staged low speed impacts indicate that mild whiplash symptoms can occur without a
L275@P10: person’s head exceeding the normal range of motion. This means that our previous focus
L276@P10: on preventing neck hyperextension is insufficient to adequately protect all rear impact
L277@P10: victims from risks of whiplash injuries. Instead, to effectively prevent whiplash, the head
L278@P10: restraint must control smaller amounts of rapid head and neck movement relative to the
L279@P10: torso.
L280@P10: In sum, in light of recent evidence that whiplash may be caused by smaller
L281@P10: amounts of head and neck movements relative to the torso, and that reduced backset and
L282@P10: increased height of head restraints help to better control these head and neck movements,
L283@P10: we conclude that head restraints should be higher and positioned closer to the occupant’s
L284@P10: head in order to be more effective in preventing whiplash.
L285@P10:  Further, information about consumer practices regarding the positioning of
L286@P10: adjustable head restraints indicates that there is a need to improve consumer awareness
L287@P10: and knowledge of importance of properly adjusted head restraints. Specifically, in 1995,
L288@P10: NHTSA surveyed 282 vehicles to examine how well head restraints were adjusted and if
L289@P10: the restraints should have been adjusted higher. Approximately 50 percent of adjustable
L290@P10: head restraints were left in the lowest adjustable position. Three quarters of these could
L291@P10: have been raised to decrease whiplash potential by bringing the head restraint higher in
L292@P10: relation to the center of gravity of the occupant's head.
L293@P10: III. Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
L294@P10: Using the new information gained about the effectiveness of head restraints,
L295@P10: NHTSA published the NPRM for this final rule to improve on the effectiveness of head
L296@P10-11: restraints. The continued persistence of high numbers of whiplash injuries indicated a 12
L297@P11: need for the rulemaking.
L298@P11: The NPRM proposed new height and backset requirements, and other
L299@P11: requirements, described below. NHTSA also proposed that head restraints be required in
L300@P11: the rear outboard seating positions.
L301@P11: In the proposed FMVSS No. 202a, manufacturers were given the option of
L302@P11: meeting either of two sets of requirements. The first set is a comprehensive group of
L303@P11: dimension and strength requirements, compliance with which is measured statically. The
L304@P11: second set was made of requirements that would have to be met in a dynamic test. 13
L305@P11: Proposed requirements for head restraints tested statically.
L306@P11: To ensure that head restraints would be properly used in a position high enough to
L307@P11: limit hyperextension, the NPRM proposed the following height requirements. The top of
L308@P11: the front integral head restraint would have to reach the height of at least 800 mm above
L309@P11: the H-point. The top of the front adjustable head restraint would have to reach the height
L310@P11: of at least 800 mm above the H-point, and could not be adjusted below 750 mm. The top
L311@P11: of the rear mandatory head restraint would have to reach the height of at least 750 mm
L312@P11: above the H-point. The NPRM also proposed that adjustable head restraints must lock in
L313@P11: their adjustment positions. NHTSA proposed to retain existing requirements for head
L314@P11: restraint width.14 To control even smaller amounts of rapid head and neck movement
L315@P11: relative to the torso than the amount of relative motion resulting in neck hyperextension,
L316@P11: the NPRM proposed also to limit the amount of backset to 50 mm (2 in). In addition, the
L317@P11: NPRM also proposed maximum gap requirements for head restraints openings within the

L356@P13: IV. Summary of Comments on the NPRM
L357@P13: The agency received approximately 50 comments on the NPRM, from motor
